paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a woman who baked five pies. When they came out of the oven, they were so overbaked that the crusts were too hard to eat. So she said to her daughter:
“Daughter,” she said, “put those pies on the shelf and leave them there for a little while, and they’ll come again.” She meant, you know, that the crusts would soften.
But the girl said to herself, “Well, if they’ll come again, I’ll eat them now.” And she set to work and ate every one of them.
Well, at suppertime the woman said, “Go and get one of those pies. I dare say they’ve come again by now.”
The girl went and looked, and there was nothing but the dishes. So she came back and said, “No, they haven’t come again.”
“Not one of them?” her mother asked.
“Not one of them,” she said.
“Well, whether they’ve come again or not,” the woman said, “I’ll have one for supper.”
“But you can’t if they haven’t come,” the girl said.
“But I can,” her mother said. “Go and bring the best one.”
“Best or worst,” the girl said, “I’ve eaten them all, and you can’t have one until it comes again.”
Well, the woman did not know what to do. She took her spinning to the doorway, and as she spun, she sang:

“My daughter has eaten five, five pies today.
My daughter has eaten five, five pies today.”
The king was coming down the street. He heard her singing but could not make out the words, so he stopped and said:
“What was that you were singing, my good woman?”
The woman was ashamed to let him hear what her daughter had done, so instead she sang:

“My daughter has spun five, five skeins today.
My daughter has spun five, five skeins today.”
“My stars!” the king said. “I’ve never heard of anyone who could do that.”

Then he said, “Now listen. I want a wife, and I’ll marry your daughter. But listen to this,” he said. “For eleven months of the year, she can have all she wants to eat, all the gowns she wants to wear, and all the company she wants to keep. But in the last month of the year, she must spin five skeins every day. And if she doesn’t, I’ll kill her.”

“All right,” the woman said, thinking what a grand marriage it would be. As for the five skeins, when the time came, there would be plenty of ways to get out of it. Most likely, he would have forgotten all about it.
Well, they were married. For eleven months the girl had all she wanted to eat, all the gowns she wanted to wear, and all the company she wanted to keep.
But as that time drew to an end, she began thinking about the skeins and wondering whether he remembered them. He said not a word about them, though, and she thought he had forgotten them altogether.

Then, on the last day of that final month, he took her to a room she had never seen before. There was nothing in it but a spinning wheel and a stool. “Now, my dear,” he said, “tomorrow you’ll be shut in here with some food and some flax. If you haven’t spun five skeins by nightfall, your head will come off.”
And away he went about his business.

Well, she was terribly frightened. She had always been such a thoughtless girl that she did not even know how to spin. What was she to do tomorrow, with no one allowed near her to help? She sat on a stool in the kitchen, and goodness, how she cried!

Then, all of a sudden, she heard a sort of knocking low down on the door. She got up and opened it. What should she see but a tiny black thing with a long tail! It looked up at her very curiously and said:
“What are you crying for?”
“What’s that to you?” she said.
“Never mind that,” it said. “Just tell me what you’re crying for.”
“It won’t do me any good to tell you,” she said.
“You don’t know that,” it said, twirling its tail.
“Well,” she said, “it won’t do any harm, even if it does no good.” And she told it about the pies, and the skeins, and everything.
“Here’s what I’ll do,” the little black thing said. “I’ll come to your window every morning and take the flax, and bring it back spun at night.”
“What do you want in payment?” she asked.
It looked at her out of the corners of its eyes and said, “I’ll give you three guesses every night to guess my name. If you haven’t guessed it by the end of the month, you’ll be mine.”
Well, she thought she was sure to guess its name before the month ended. “All right,” she said. “I agree.”
“All right,” it said. And goodness, how it twirled its tail!
The next day her husband took her into the room. The flax and the day’s food were there.
“There’s the flax,” he said. “If it isn’t spun by tonight, off goes your head.” Then he went out and locked the door.
He had barely left when there was a knock at the window.
She got up and opened it, and sure enough, there was the little old creature sitting on the ledge.
“Where’s the flax?” he asked.
“Here it is,” she said, and gave it to him.
Well, that evening there was another knock at the window. She got up and opened it, and there was the little old creature with five skeins of flax on his arm.
“Here it is,” he said, and handed it to her.
“Now, what’s my name?” he asked.
“Is it Bill?” she said.
“No, it isn’t,” he said, twirling his tail.
“Is it Ned?” she asked.
“No, it isn’t,” he said, twirling his tail.
“Well, is it Mark?” she asked.
“No, it isn’t,” he said, twirling his tail harder. And away he flew.
Well, when her husband came in, the five skeins were ready for him. “I see I won’t have to kill you tonight, my dear,” he said. “You’ll have your food and your flax in the morning.” And away he went.

Every day the flax and the food were brought, and every morning and evening that little black imp came. All day long, the girl sat trying to think of names to say to him when he came at night. But she never hit on the right one. As the end of the month drew nearer, the imp began to look so spiteful, and his tail twirled faster and faster each time she guessed.
At last the second-to-last day arrived. The imp came at night with the five skeins and said:
“What, haven’t you guessed my name yet?”
“Is it Nicodemus?” she asked.
“No, it isn’t,” he said.
“Is it Sammle?” she asked.
“No, it isn’t,” he said.
“Well then, is it Methusalem?” she asked.
“No, it isn’t that either,” he said.
Then he looked at her with eyes like burning coals and said, “Woman, there’s only tomorrow night left, and then you’ll be mine!” And away he flew.
Well, she felt dreadful. Then she heard the king coming along the passage. In he came, and when he saw the five skeins, he said:

“Well, my dear, I see no reason why you won’t have your skeins ready tomorrow night too. Since I don’t suppose I’ll have to kill you, I’ll have supper here tonight.” So they brought supper and another stool for him, and the two of them sat down.
He had eaten only a mouthful or so when he stopped and began to laugh.
“What is it?” she asked.

“Well,” he said, “I was out hunting today, and I found myself in a part of the wood I had never seen before. There was an old chalk pit there, and I heard a sort of humming. So I got off my small horse, walked very quietly to the pit, and looked down. What should I see but the funniest little black thing you ever laid eyes on! And what was it doing? It had a little spinning wheel and was spinning wonderfully fast, twirling its tail. And as it spun, it sang:

“Nimmy nimmy not,
My name’s Tom Tit Tot.”
When the girl heard this, she felt as though she could jump out of her skin for joy, but she did not say a word.

The next day, that little creature looked so spiteful when he came for the flax. When night came, she heard him knocking against the windowpanes. She opened the window, and he came right in onto the ledge. He was grinning from ear to ear, and oh, his tail was twirling so fast!
“What’s my name?” he asked as he handed her the skeins.
“Is it Solomon?” she asked, pretending to be afraid.
“No, it isn’t,” he said, moving farther into the room.
“Well, is it Zebedee?” she asked again.
“No, it isn’t,” the imp said. Then he laughed and twirled his tail until she could hardly see it.
“Take your time, woman,” he said. “One more guess, and you’re mine.” He stretched his black hands towards her.
She stepped back a pace or two and looked at him. Then she laughed aloud and said, pointing at him:
“NIMMY NIMMY NOT, YOUR NAME’S TOM TIT TOT!”
When he heard her, he gave a dreadful shriek and flew away into the dark. She never saw him again.
